{{Short description|Solutions of the Laplace equation in spherical polar coordinates}}
In [[physics]] and [[mathematics]], the '''solid harmonics''' are solutions of the [[Laplace equation]] in [[spherical polar coordinates]], assumed to be (smooth) functions <math>\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{C}</math>. There are two kinds: the ''regular solid harmonics'' <math>R^m_\ell(\mathbf{r})</math>, which are well-defined at the origin and the ''irregular solid harmonics'' <math>I^m_{\ell}(\mathbf{r})</math>, which are singular at the origin. Both sets of functions play an important role in [[potential theory]], and are obtained by rescaling [[spherical harmonics]] appropriately:<math display="block"> 
R^m_{\ell}(\mathbf{r}) \equiv \sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{2\ell+1}}\; r^\ell Y^m_{\ell}(\theta,\varphi)
</math>
<math display="block"> 
I^m_{\ell}(\mathbf{r}) \equiv \sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{2\ell+1}} \; \frac{ Y^m_{\ell}(\theta,\varphi)}{r^{\ell+1}}
</math>

== Derivation, relation to spherical harmonics ==
Introducing {{mvar|r}}, {{mvar|θ}}, and {{mvar|φ}} for the spherical polar coordinates of the 3-vector {{math|'''r'''}}, and assuming that <math>\Phi</math> is a (smooth) function <math>\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{C}</math>, we can write the Laplace equation in the following form
<math display="block"> \nabla^2\Phi(\mathbf{r}) =  \left(\frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial r^2}r - \frac{\hat L^2}{r^2}\right)\Phi(\mathbf{r}) = 0 , \qquad \mathbf{r} \ne \mathbf{0},
</math>
where {{math|''L''<sup>2</sup>}} is the square of the {{Em|nondimensional}} [[angular momentum operator]],
<math display="block"> \mathbf{\hat L} = -i\, (\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{\nabla}) .
</math>

It is [[Angular momentum#Relation to spherical harmonics|known]] that [[spherical harmonics]] {{math|''Y''{{su|p=''m''|b=''ℓ''|lh=1em}}}} are eigenfunctions of {{math|''L''<sup>2</sup>}}:
<math display="block">
\hat L^2 Y^m_{\ell}\equiv \left[ \hat L_x^2 + \hat L_y^2 + \hat L_z^2\right] Y^m_{\ell} = \ell (\ell+1) Y^m_{\ell}.
</math>

Substitution of {{math|1=Φ('''r''') = ''F''(''r'') ''Y''{{su|p=''m''|b=''ℓ''|lh=1em}}}} into the Laplace equation gives, after dividing out the spherical [[harmonic function]], the following  radial equation and its general solution,

<math display="block">
\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial r^2}r F(r) = \frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{r^2} F(r)
\Longrightarrow F(r) = A r^\ell + B r^{-\ell-1}.
</math>

The particular solutions of the total Laplace equation are '''regular solid harmonics''':
<math display="block">
R^m_{\ell}(\mathbf{r}) \equiv \sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{2\ell+1}}\; r^\ell Y^m_{\ell}(\theta,\varphi), 
</math>
and  '''irregular solid harmonics''':
<math display="block">
I^m_{\ell}(\mathbf{r}) \equiv \sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{2\ell+1}} \; \frac{ Y^m_{\ell}(\theta,\varphi)}{r^{\ell+1}} .
</math>
The regular solid harmonics correspond to [[harmonic functions|harmonic]] [[homogeneous polynomials]], i.e. homogeneous polynomials which are solutions to [[Laplace's equation]].

===Racah's normalization===
[[Giulio Racah|Racah]]'s normalization (also known as Schmidt's semi-normalization) is applied to both functions 
<math display="block">
\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin\theta\, d\theta \int_0^{2\pi} d\varphi\; R^m_{\ell}(\mathbf{r})^*\; R^m_{\ell}(\mathbf{r}) 
=  \frac{4\pi}{2\ell+1} r^{2\ell}
</math>
(and analogously for the irregular solid harmonic) instead of normalization to unity. This is convenient because in many applications the Racah normalization factor appears unchanged throughout the derivations.

==Addition theorems==
The translation of the regular solid harmonic gives a finite expansion,
<math display="block"> R^m_\ell(\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{a}) = \sum_{\lambda=0}^\ell\binom{2\ell}{2\lambda}^{1/2} \sum_{\mu=-\lambda}^\lambda R^\mu_{\lambda}(\mathbf{r}) R^{m-\mu}_{\ell-\lambda}(\mathbf{a})\;
\langle \lambda, \mu; \ell-\lambda, m-\mu| \ell m \rangle,
</math>
where the [[Clebsch–Gordan coefficient]] is given by
<math display="block">
\langle \lambda, \mu; \ell-\lambda, m-\mu| \ell m \rangle
= \binom{\ell+m}{\lambda+\mu}^{1/2} \binom{\ell-m}{\lambda-\mu}^{1/2} \binom{2\ell}{2\lambda}^{-1/2}.
</math>

The similar expansion for irregular solid harmonics gives an [[Series (mathematics)|infinite series]],
<math display="block"> I^m_\ell(\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{a}) = \sum_{\lambda=0}^\infty\binom{2\ell+2\lambda+1}{2\lambda}^{1/2} \sum_{\mu=-\lambda}^\lambda R^\mu_{\lambda}(\mathbf{r}) I^{m-\mu}_{\ell+\lambda}(\mathbf{a})\;
\langle \lambda, \mu; \ell+\lambda, m-\mu| \ell m \rangle
</math>
with <math> |r| \le |a|\,</math>. The quantity between pointed brackets is again a [[Clebsch-Gordan coefficient]],
<math display="block">
\langle \lambda, \mu; \ell+\lambda, m-\mu| \ell m \rangle
= (-1)^{\lambda+\mu}\binom{\ell+\lambda-m+\mu}{\lambda+\mu}^{1/2} \binom{\ell+\lambda+m-\mu}{\lambda-\mu}^{1/2}
\binom{2\ell+2\lambda+1}{2\lambda}^{-1/2}.
</math>

The addition theorems were proved in different manners by several authors.<ref> R. J. A. Tough and A. J. Stone, J. Phys. A: Math. Gen. Vol. '''10''', p.&nbsp;1261 (1977)</ref><ref> M. J. Caola, J. Phys. A: Math. Gen. Vol. '''11''', p.&nbsp;L23 (1978)</ref>

==Complex form==
The regular solid harmonics are homogeneous, polynomial solutions to the Laplace equation <math>\Delta R=0</math>. Separating the indeterminate <math>z</math> and writing <math display="inline">R = \sum_a p_a(x,y) z^a</math>, the Laplace equation is easily seen to be equivalent to the recursion formula
<math display="block">p_{a+2} = \frac{-\left(\partial_x^2 + \partial_y^2\right) p_a}{\left(a+2\right) \left(a+1\right)}</math>
so that any choice of polynomials <math>p_0(x,y)</math> of degree <math> \ell</math> and <math>p_1(x,y)</math> of degree <math>\ell-1</math> gives a solution to the equation. One particular basis of the space of homogeneous polynomials (in two variables) of degree <math>k</math> is <math>\left\{(x^2+y^2)^m(x\pm iy)^{k-2m} \mid 0\leq m\leq k/2\right\}</math>. Note that it is the (unique up to normalization) basis of [[eigenvector]]s of the rotation group <math>SO(2)</math>: The rotation <math>\rho_\alpha</math> of the plane by <math>\alpha\in[0,2\pi]</math> acts as multiplication by <math>e^{\pm i(k-2m)\alpha}</math> on the basis vector <math>(x^2+y^2)^m (x+iy)^{k-2m}</math>.

If we combine the degree <math>\ell</math> basis and the degree <math>\ell-1</math> basis with the recursion formula, we obtain a basis of the space of harmonic, homogeneous polynomials (in three variables this time) of degree <math>\ell</math> consisting of eigenvectors for <math>SO(2)</math> (note that the recursion formula is compatible with the <math>SO(2)</math>-action because the Laplace operator is rotationally invariant). These are the complex solid harmonics:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
R_\ell^{\pm\ell} &= (x \pm iy)^\ell z^0 \\
R_\ell^{\pm(\ell-1)} &= (x \pm iy)^{\ell-1} z^1 \\
R_\ell^{\pm(\ell-2)} &= (x^2+y^2)(x \pm iy)^{\ell-2} z^0 + \frac{-(\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2)\left( (x^2+y^2)(x \pm iy)^{\ell-2} \right)}{1\cdot 2} z^2 \\
R_\ell^{\pm(\ell-3)} &= (x^2+y^2)(x \pm iy)^{\ell-3} z^1 + \frac{-(\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2)\left( (x^2+y^2)(x \pm iy)^{\ell-3} \right)}{2\cdot 3} z^3 \\
R_\ell^{\pm(\ell-4)} &= (x^2+y^2)^2(x \pm iy)^{\ell-4} z^0 + \frac{-(\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2)\left( (x^2+y^2)^2(x \pm iy)^{\ell-4} \right)}{1\cdot 2} z^2 + \frac{ (\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2)^2 \left( (x^2+y^2)^2(x \pm iy)^{\ell-4}\right)}{1\cdot 2 \cdot 3\cdot 4}z^4 \\
R_\ell^{\pm(\ell-5)} &= (x^2+y^2)^2(x \pm iy)^{\ell-5} z^1 + \frac{-(\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2)\left( (x^2+y^2)^2(x \pm iy)^{\ell-5} \right)}{2\cdot 3} z^3 + \frac{ (\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2)^2 \left( (x^2+y^2)^2(x \pm iy)^{\ell-5}\right)}{2 \cdot 3\cdot 4\cdot 5}z^5 \\
&\;\,\vdots
\end{align}</math>
and in general
<math display="block">R_\ell^{\pm m} = \begin{cases}
\sum_k (\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2)^k \left( (x^2+y^2)^{(\ell-m)/2} (x\pm iy)^m \right) \frac{(-1)^k z^{2k}}{ (2k)! } & \ell-m \text{ is even} \\
\sum_k (\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2)^k \left( (x^2+y^2)^{(\ell-1-m)/2} (x\pm iy)^m \right) \frac{(-1)^k z^{2k+1}}{ (2k+1)! } & \ell-m \text{ is odd}
\end{cases}</math>
for <math>0\leq m\leq \ell</math>.

Plugging in [[spherical coordinates]] <math>x = r\cos(\theta)\sin(\varphi)</math>, <math>y = r\sin(\theta)\sin(\varphi)</math>, <math>z = r\cos(\varphi)</math> and using <math>x^2+y^2=r^2 \sin(\varphi)^2 = r^2(1-\cos(\varphi)^2)</math> one finds the usual relationship to spherical harmonics <math>R_\ell^m = r^\ell e^{im\phi} P_\ell^m(\cos(\vartheta))</math> with a polynomial <math>P_\ell^m</math>, which is (up to normalization) the [[associated Legendre polynomial]], and so <math>R_\ell^m = r^\ell Y_\ell^m(\theta,\varphi)</math> (again, up to the specific choice of normalization).

==Real form==
{{Unreferenced section|date=October 2010}}
By a simple linear combination of solid harmonics of {{math|±''m''}} these functions are transformed into real functions, i.e. functions <math>\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}</math>.  The real regular solid harmonics,  expressed in Cartesian  coordinates, are real-valued homogeneous polynomials of order <math>\ell</math> in ''x'', ''y'', ''z''. The explicit form of these polynomials is of some importance. They appear, for example, in the form of spherical [[atomic orbital]]s and real [[multipole moments]]. The explicit Cartesian expression of the real regular harmonics will now be derived.

===Linear combination ===

We write in agreement with the earlier definition 
<math display="block">
R_\ell^m(r,\theta,\varphi) = (-1)^{(m+|m|)/2}\; r^\ell \;\Theta_{\ell}^{|m|} (\cos\theta)
 e^{im\varphi}, \qquad -\ell \le m \le \ell,
</math>
with
<math display="block">
\Theta_{\ell}^m (\cos\theta) \equiv \left[\frac{(\ell-m)!}{(\ell+m)!}\right]^{1/2} \,\sin^m\theta\, \frac{d^m P_\ell(\cos\theta)}{d\cos^m\theta}, \qquad m\ge 0,
</math>
where <math> P_\ell(\cos\theta)</math> is a [[Legendre polynomial]] of order {{mvar|ℓ}}.
The {{mvar|m}} dependent phase is known as the [[Spherical harmonics#Condon–Shortley phase|Condon–Shortley phase]].

The following expression defines the real regular solid harmonics:
<math display="block">
\begin{pmatrix}
C_\ell^{m} \\
S_\ell^{m}
\end{pmatrix}
\equiv \sqrt{2} \; r^\ell \; \Theta^{m}_\ell
\begin{pmatrix}
\cos m\varphi\\ \sin m\varphi
\end{pmatrix} 
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{pmatrix}
(-1)^m  & \quad 1 \\
-(-1)^m i & \quad i 
\end{pmatrix} 
\begin{pmatrix}
R_\ell^{m} \\
R_\ell^{-m}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad m > 0.
</math>
and for {{math|1=''m'' = 0}}:
<math display="block">C_\ell^0 \equiv R_\ell^0 .</math>
Since the transformation is by a [[unitary matrix]] the normalization of the real and the complex solid harmonics is the same.

=== ''z''-dependent part ===

Upon writing {{math|1=''u'' = cos ''θ''}} the {{mvar|m}}-th derivative of the Legendre polynomial can be written as the following expansion in {{mvar|u}}
<math display="block">
\frac{d^m P_\ell(u)}{du^m} =
\sum_{k=0}^{\left \lfloor (\ell-m)/2\right \rfloor} \gamma^{(m)}_{\ell k}\; u^{\ell-2k-m}
</math>
with
<math display="block">
\gamma^{(m)}_{\ell k} = (-1)^k 2^{-\ell} \binom{\ell}{k}\binom{2\ell-2k}{\ell} \frac{(\ell-2k)!}{(\ell-2k-m)!}.
</math>
Since {{math|1=''z'' = ''r'' cos ''θ''}} it follows that this derivative, times an appropriate power of {{mvar|r}}, is a simple polynomial in {{mvar|z}},
<math display="block">
\Pi^m_\ell(z)\equiv
r^{\ell-m} \frac{d^m P_\ell(u)}{du^m} =
\sum_{k=0}^{\left \lfloor (\ell-m)/2\right \rfloor} \gamma^{(m)}_{\ell k}\; r^{2k}\; z^{\ell-2k-m}.
</math>

=== (''x'',''y'')-dependent part ===

Consider next, recalling that {{math|1=''x'' = ''r'' sin ''θ'' cos ''φ''}} and {{math|1=''y'' = ''r'' sin ''θ'' sin ''φ''}},
<math display="block">
r^m \sin^m\theta \cos m\varphi = \frac{1}{2} \left[  (r \sin\theta e^{i\varphi})^m 
+ (r \sin\theta e^{-i\varphi})^m \right] =
\frac{1}{2} \left[  (x+iy)^m + (x-iy)^m \right]
</math>
Likewise
<math display="block">
r^m \sin^m\theta \sin m\varphi = \frac{1}{2i} \left[  (r \sin\theta e^{i\varphi})^m 
- (r \sin\theta e^{-i\varphi})^m \right] =
\frac{1}{2i} \left[  (x+iy)^m - (x-iy)^m \right].
</math>
Further
<math display="block">
A_m(x,y) \equiv
\frac{1}{2} \left[  (x+iy)^m + (x-iy)^m \right]= \sum_{p=0}^m \binom{m}{p} x^p y^{m-p} \cos (m-p) \frac{\pi}{2}
</math>
and
<math display="block">
B_m(x,y) \equiv
\frac{1}{2i} \left[  (x+iy)^m - (x-iy)^m \right]= \sum_{p=0}^m \binom{m}{p} x^p y^{m-p} \sin (m-p) \frac{\pi}{2}.
</math>

===In total ===

<math display="block">
C^m_\ell(x,y,z) = \left[\frac{(2-\delta_{m0}) (\ell-m)!}{(\ell+m)!}\right]^{1/2} \Pi^m_{\ell}(z)\;A_m(x,y),\qquad m=0,1, \ldots,\ell
</math>
<math display="block">
S^m_\ell(x,y,z) = \left[\frac{2 (\ell-m)!}{(\ell+m)!}\right]^{1/2} \Pi^m_{\ell}(z)\;B_m(x,y)
,\qquad m=1,2,\ldots,\ell.
</math>

=== List of lowest functions ===

We list explicitly the lowest functions up to and including {{math|1=''ℓ'' = 5}}.
Here <math>\bar{\Pi}^m_\ell(z) \equiv \left[\tfrac{(2-\delta_{m0}) (\ell-m)!}{(\ell+m)!}\right]^{1/2} \Pi^m_{\ell}(z) .
</math>

<math display="block">
 \begin{align}
 \bar{\Pi}^0_0 & = 1   &
      \bar{\Pi}^1_3 & = \frac{1}{4}\sqrt{6}(5z^2-r^2)  &
            \bar{\Pi}^4_4 & = \frac{1}{8}\sqrt{35}  \\
 \bar{\Pi}^0_1 & = z   &
      \bar{\Pi}^2_3 & = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{15}\; z    &
            \bar{\Pi}^0_5 & = \frac{1}{8}z(63z^4-70z^2r^2+15r^4) \\
 \bar{\Pi}^1_1 & = 1   &
      \bar{\Pi}^3_3 & = \frac{1}{4}\sqrt{10}        &
            \bar{\Pi}^1_5 & = \frac{1}{8}\sqrt{15} (21z^4-14z^2r^2+r^4) \\
 \bar{\Pi}^0_2 & = \frac{1}{2}(3z^2-r^2) &
      \bar{\Pi}^0_4 & = \frac{1}{8}(35 z^4-30 r^2 z^2 +3r^4 ) &
            \bar{\Pi}^2_5 & = \frac{1}{4}\sqrt{105}(3z^2-r^2)z \\
 \bar{\Pi}^1_2 & = \sqrt{3}z &
      \bar{\Pi}^1_4 & = \frac{\sqrt{10}}{4} z(7z^2-3r^2) &
            \bar{\Pi}^3_5 & = \frac{1}{16}\sqrt{70} (9z^2-r^2) \\
 \bar{\Pi}^2_2 & = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{3}  &
      \bar{\Pi}^2_4 & = \frac{1}{4}\sqrt{5}(7z^2-r^2)  &
            \bar{\Pi}^4_5 & = \frac{3}{8}\sqrt{35} z  \\
 \bar{\Pi}^0_3 & = \frac{1}{2} z(5z^2-3r^2) &
      \bar{\Pi}^3_4 & = \frac{1}{4}\sqrt{70}\;z  &
            \bar{\Pi}^5_5 & = \frac{3}{16}\sqrt{14} \\
 \end{align}
</math>

The lowest functions <math>A_m(x,y)\,</math> and <math> B_m(x,y)\,</math> are:
